subject: chemistry
title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
key_idea: An aqueous solution contains the ions of the compound and also H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from water. At the cathode, hydrogen forms if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen forms unless the solution contains halide ions.

blocks.text: This section covers why a solution has more ions than the compound alone.

items.meaning: An ion that gains or loses electrons at an electrode and forms an atom or molecule.
A negative ion of a halogen, such as chloride, bromide or iodide.

items: Water molecules break down to produce **hydrogen ions** (H⁺) and **hydroxide ions** (OH⁻).
So the solution has two positive ions and two negative ions.
Only one ion is discharged at each electrode.
Which ion is discharged depends on the reactivity of the elements involved.
Water adds H⁺ and OH⁻ ions to every aqueous solution.
One ion is discharged at each electrode.

blocks.text: This section covers the rules for the product at each electrode, using inert electrodes and a solution of one compound.

items: If the metal is **more reactive than hydrogen**, hydrogen forms. Sodium and potassium solutions give hydrogen.
If the metal is **less reactive than hydrogen**, the metal forms. Copper solutions give copper.
Hydrogen is seen as bubbles. It burns with a squeaky pop.
Copper is seen as a pink-brown solid on the electrode.
If the solution contains **halide ions**, the halogen forms. Chloride gives chlorine, bromide gives bromine and iodide gives iodine.
If there are no halide ions, **oxygen** forms. Sulfate and nitrate solutions give oxygen.
Chlorine and oxygen are seen as bubbles. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.

diagram.alt: Choose a salt solution to see the products of electrolysis at each electrode.

options.label: Sodium chloride
results: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen. Chloride is a halide.
options.explanation: Na⁺ and OH⁻ are left in solution, so the solution becomes alkaline.

options.label: Copper sulfate
results: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen. There is no halide.

options.label: Sodium sulfate
results: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen. There is no halide.

options.label: Copper chloride
results: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen. Chloride is a halide.

options.label: Potassium bromide
results: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen. Bromide is a halide.

options.label: Potassium iodide
results: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen. Iodide is a halide.

items: Negative electrode: hydrogen if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, otherwise the metal.
Positive electrode: a halogen if there is a halide ion, otherwise oxygen.

sections.heading: Explaining why hydrogen or oxygen forms

blocks.text: This section covers the explanation that exam questions ask for.

items: Water breaks down to produce H⁺ ions.
H⁺ ions are attracted to the negative electrode.
The metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead of the metal ions. Hydrogen forms.
(Higher tier) H⁺ ions gain electrons. They are reduced.
Water breaks down to produce OH⁻ ions.
OH⁻ ions are attracted to the positive electrode.
There is no halide in the solution, so OH⁻ ions are discharged. Oxygen forms.
(Higher tier) OH⁻ ions lose electrons. They are oxidised.
In sodium chloride solution, H⁺ ions are discharged at the negative electrode and Cl⁻ ions at the positive electrode.
Sodium ions and hydroxide ions are left in the solution.
The solution becomes alkaline, so its pH increases.
H⁺ and OH⁻ ions come from water.
The metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is made instead of the metal.
Sodium chloride solution is left alkaline, because OH⁻ ions remain.

checks.q: Name the product at each electrode when potassium bromide solution is electrolysed.
checks.a: Negative electrode: hydrogen. Positive electrode: bromine.

checks.q: Explain why sodium is not made when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.
checks.a: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged and hydrogen is produced instead.

checks.q: Describe what is seen at each electrode when copper chloride solution is electrolysed.
checks.a: Positive electrode: bubbles (of chlorine). Negative electrode: a pink-brown solid (copper).

worked_example.question:
Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas are produced when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed.

Explain how oxygen gas is produced in the electrolysis of sodium sulfate solution.
answer_points: break down to produce OH⁻ ions.
The OH⁻ ions are attracted to the positive electrode.
Where the OH⁻ ions are oxidised (lose electrons).
worked_example.tip: One mark for each step. 'Discharged' is ignored, so say oxidised or lose electrons.

worked_example.question:
Water, acidified with sulfuric acid, is decomposed by electrolysis. The water is decomposed to produce hydrogen and oxygen.

Throughout the experiment the volume of hydrogen and the volume of oxygen are measured at two-minute intervals.

Time in minutes: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Volume of hydrogen in cm³: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16
Volume of oxygen in cm³: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8

Describe, using the data, what the results show about the volumes of hydrogen and of oxygen produced in this experiment.
answer_points: The volumes of hydrogen and oxygen increase with time (directly proportional to time).
The volume of hydrogen is double the volume of oxygen: a 2 : 1 ratio, or twice as much hydrogen as oxygen.
worked_example.tip: Refer to the ratio explicitly. Quoting two figures is not enough.

blocks.text: Edexcel also asks about the electrolysis of water that has been acidified with sulfuric acid, using inert electrodes.

items: Hydrogen forms at the negative electrode.
Oxygen forms at the positive electrode.
The volume of hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen, a ratio of 2 : 1.
Graphite electrodes are used because they are inert and conduct electricity.

worked_example.question:
A teacher electrolyses aqueous sodium chloride, NaCl, and measures the volume of hydrogen gas given off.

A student repeats the experiment with aqueous copper sulfate, CuSO₄. The student finds that no hydrogen gas is given off.

Explain why hydrogen gas is given off in the electrolysis of aqueous NaCl, but not in the electrolysis of aqueous CuSO₄.
answer_points: Hydrogen is produced at the cathode if ions of a metal more reactive than hydrogen are present. Only one ion is discharged at each electrode, based on the reactivity series.
Hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, so hydrogen is formed from NaCl solution.
Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper is formed from CuSO₄ solution.
worked_example.tip: Name both metals and compare each with hydrogen.

worked_example.question:
Ionic compounds can be decomposed by the passage of an electric current using inert electrodes.
Name the products and state the observations at the negative and positive electrodes when dilute aqueous potassium bromide, KBr, is decomposed by the passage of an electric current.
product at the negative electrode ______
observations at the negative electrode ______
products at the positive electrode ______ and ______
observations at the positive electrode ______
answer_points: Product at the negative electrode: hydrogen.
Observation at the negative electrode: bubbles.
Products at the positive electrode: oxygen and water.
Observation at the positive electrode: bubbles.
worked_example.tip: The solution is dilute, so oxygen forms at the positive electrode, not bromine.

blocks.text: The anode product of a halide solution depends on its concentration.

items: (Supplement) A **concentrated** halide solution gives the halogen at the positive electrode.
(Supplement) A **dilute** halide solution gives oxygen at the positive electrode, and water forms too.
Hydrogen forms at the negative electrode in both.

rows: Chlorine: bubbles of a pale yellow-green gas

worked_example.question:
When copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes, copper forms at the negative electrode.
State the appearance of the copper that forms on the negative electrode.
answer_points: A pink (or pink-brown) solid coating on the electrode.

items: Dilute sulfuric acid gives hydrogen at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive electrode.
Bubbles are seen at both electrodes.
The electrodes must be inert. Zinc electrodes would react with the acid, so platinum or graphite is used.
